identity.title: CO line observations of OH/IR stars in the inner Galactic Bulge: Characteristics of stars at the tip of the AGB

paper_type_evidence.quote: Our goal is to characterise the stellar and circumstellar properties of high-mass-loss-rate OH/IR stars in the inner Galactic Bulge using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Interferometer (ALMA).
Rotational lines of $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO, as well as a millimetre-wave continuum, have been observed for a sample of 22 OH/IR stars in directions within 2$^\circ$ of the Galactic Centre.

question.value: Characterise the stellar and circumstellar properties (luminosities, mass-loss rates, expansion velocities, gas-to-dust ratios, and 12CO/13CO abundance ratios) of high-mass-loss-rate OH/IR stars in the inner Galactic Bulge.

evidence.quote: Our goal is to characterise the stellar and circumstellar properties of high-mass-loss-rate OH/IR stars in the inner Galactic Bulge using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Interferometer (ALMA).
This paper makes use of the following ALMA data: ADS/JAO.ALMA#2016.1.00983.S.

The ALMA dataset consists of three different tunings to cover the $^{12}$CO $J$ = 2–1 line in Band 6 ($\approx$ 230 GHz) and the $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO $J$ = 3–2 lines in Band 7 ($\approx$ 345 and 330 GHz, respectively).

frequencies_and_spectral_setup.value: one 1.875 GHz SPW with 1920 channels (0.977 MHz spacing, 0.8-1.3 km/s native after Hann smoothing, 5 km/s final) on CO lines (~230, ~330, ~345 GHz); three 2 GHz SPWs with 128 channels (15.625 MHz spacing, 27-40 km/s) for continuum at 222, 324, 339 GHz

evidence.quote: For all tunings, the correlator was set up with one 1.875 GHz spectral window centred on the relevant CO line, with 1920 channels separated by 0.977 MHz, and three additional 2 GHz spectral windows with 128 channels and a coarser spacing of 15.625 MHz for continuum measurements

After Hann smoothing[^2], the native velocity resolution for the CO spectral windows is between 0.8 and 1.3 km s$^{-1}$. For the continuum windows, the velocity resolution is between 27 and 40 km s$^{-1}$. For analysis, the final CO line velocity resolution was set to 5 km s$^{-1}$.

The ALMA dataset consists of three different tunings to cover the $^{12}$CO $J$ = 2–1 line in Band 6 ($\approx$ 230 GHz) and the $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO $J$ = 3–2 lines in Band 7 ($\approx$ 345 and 330 GHz, respectively).

The ALMA dataset consists of three different tunings to cover the $^{12}$CO $J$ = 2–1 line in Band 6 ($\approx$ 230 GHz) and the $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO $J$ = 3–2 lines in Band 7 ($\approx$ 345 and 330 GHz, respectively).

The $^{12}$CO($J$ = 3–2) setting also allowed detection of the H$^{13}$CN($J$ = 4–3) line at 345.3398 GHz.

evidence.quote: For the continuum this means three measurements with 6 GHz bandwidth centred at the effective frequencies of 222, 324, and 339 GHz for each source.

The observations were performed in array configurations with baselines ranging between $\approx$ 20 m to 2 $-$ 3 km.

angular_resolution.value: 0.16''-0.18'' (typically) and 0.19'' (final) in Band 6; 0.11''-0.17'' (typically) and 0.14'' (final) in Band 7

evidence.quote: The achieved synthesised beams ($\theta_{\rm b}$, the full width at half maximum, FWHM) vary, but are typically about 0.16$''$ $-$ 0.18$''$ in Band 6 and 0.11$''$ $-$ 0.17$''$ in Band 7.

sensitivity.value: Line rms (at 5 km/s): ~4 mJy/beam (13CO 3-2), ~9 mJy/beam (12CO 2-1), ~24 mJy/beam (12CO 3-2); Continuum rms: ~0.23, 0.13, and 0.65 mJy/beam at 222, 324, and 339 GHz

evidence.quote: The $^{13}$CO $J$ = 3–2 data have the highest sensitivity, the rms noise per channel in the images is $\approx$ 4 mJy beam$^{-1}$ at 5 km s$^{-1}$ resolution. The corresponding values for the $^{12}$CO $J$ = 2–1 and 3–2 data are $\approx$ 9 and 24 mJy beam$^{-1}$, respectively.
The continuum rms values are $\approx$ 0.23 mJy beam$^{-1}$, 0.13 mJy beam$^{-1}$, and 0.65 mJy beam$^{-1}$ at 222, 324, and 339 GHz, respectively.

time_on_source.value: ~12 s per target per execution for 12CO tunings; ~50 s per target per execution (x3 executions) for 13CO tuning; ~1 hour total for the whole project

evidence.quote: The $^{12}$CO tunings were observed in one execution each in October 2016, with a fast snapshot observation of about 12 s on each of the 22 targets.

The $^{13}$CO tuning was observed three times, twice in October 2016 and once in July 2017, with a longer integration time of about 50 s per target for each execution. The total amount of on-source observing time was only about an hour for the whole project.

analysis_steps.goal: Suppress interstellar CO contamination and image line and continuum emission

method.value: Image visibilities using CASA tclean with Briggs weighting (robust = 0.5). Where interstellar CO emission contaminates the line of sight, reject visibilities from shortest baselines (<25 m or <50 m) before imaging.

evidence.quote: Imaging was done using the CASA `tclean` algorithm. The final line images were created using Briggs weighting with a robust parameter of 0.5.

The presence of interstellar CO line emission along the line of sight occasionally makes it difficult to isolate the circumstellar emission. In such cases, we rejected visibility data from the shortest baselines, up to 50 m.

key_parameters.value: robust = 0.5; velocity resolution = 5 km s^-1; baseline cutoffs >25 m or >50 m for affected sources

evidence.quote: The final line images were created using Briggs weighting with a robust parameter of 0.5.
For analysis, the final CO line velocity resolution was set to 5 km s$^{-1}$.

assumptions.value: Eliminating baselines <= 50 m suppresses extended emission on scales > 5-10'' without significant loss of circumstellar flux

evidence.quote: Eliminating the shortest baselines, $\le$ 50 m (and those are in the far minority of all the baselines) will effectively suppress any extended emission on scales larger than 5$-$10$''$ .

validation.value: Isolation of 12CO circumstellar emission was guided by the less-contaminated 13CO(J=3-2) results

evidence.quote: In the case of the $^{12}$CO lines this method was used for nine sources, but here the isolation of the circumstellar emission was guided by the $^{13}$CO results.

analysis_steps.goal: Measure source positions, sizes, and continuum flux densities, and extract line profiles

method.value: Fit 2D Gaussians in the image plane to velocity-integrated line brightness distributions and continuum maps to determine positions, deconvolved FWHMs, and continuum fluxes. Extract line spectra over apertures 2-3 times the brightness distribution FWHM and fit an analytical line profile function.

evidence.quote: Hence, the sizes of the molecular envelopes cannot be determined from our data, and we report the FWHM (deconvolved with the synthesised beam) of a two-dimensional Gaussian fitted to the velocity-integrated brightness distribution.
The line profiles were extracted over an aperture, centred on the peak of the brightness distribution, larger than the estimated FWHM of the brightness distribution, normally 2–3 times larger.

The continuum brightness distributions are sharply peaked and we determine their sizes, positions, and flux densities (and their associated uncertainties) by fitting two-dimensional Gaussians to the data in the image plane.

key_parameters.value: Aperture size = 2-3 times FWHM of brightness distribution; Line shape function S(v) = S(v_c) [1 - ((v - v_c)/v_inf)^2]^beta

evidence.quote: The line profiles were extracted over an aperture, centred on the peak of the brightness distribution, larger than the estimated FWHM of the brightness distribution, normally 2–3 times larger.

Flux densities, centre velocities (in the local standard of rest frame), and expansion velocities were determined through fitting the line shape function $$\begin{equation} S(\varv) = S(\varv_{\rm c})\, \left[ 1 - \left( \frac{\varv - \varv_{\rm c}}{\varv_\infty} \right)^2 \right]^\beta \end{equation}$$ to the data

fitting.value: 2D Gaussian fitting in image plane; analytical line shape profile fitting for S(v_c), v_c, v_inf, and beta

evidence.quote: Flux densities, centre velocities (in the local standard of rest frame), and expansion velocities were determined through fitting the line shape function $$\begin{equation} S(\varv) = S(\varv_{\rm c})\, \left[ 1 - \left( \frac{\varv - \varv_{\rm c}}{\varv_\infty} \right)^2 \right]^\beta \end{equation}$$ to the data

evidence.quote: The median and maximum offsets between the $^{13}$CO($J$ = 3–2) and near-IR positions are 0.11$''$ and 0.23$''$, respectively.
The median and maximum offsets between the $^{13}$CO($J$ = 3–2) and 324 GHz continuum positions are 0.02$''$ and 0.12$''$, respectively

analysis_steps.goal: Construct extinction-corrected SEDs and determine pulsation periods

method.value: Gather archival photometry (1-30+ um), correct for interstellar extinction up to 30 um using reddening maps and extinction laws, and analyse VVV Ks and WISE W1/W2 light curves to determine single pulsation periods.

evidence.quote: The reddening is converted into extinction in the $K_{\rm s}$ band, $A_{K_{\rm s}}$ given in Table 2, and extrapolated up to 8 $\mu$m using the relationships provided by (cite: nishetal09). In the range 8 to 30 $\mu$m we use the results of (cite: wangetal15) and (cite: xueetal16).

The $K_{\rm s}$-band light curves have been analysed using the codes and methodology outlined in (cite: groeetal20) assuming a single period. For the WISE data a very similar approach was adopted to analyse the light curves in the W1 (3.4 $\mu$m) and W2 (4.6 $\mu$m) bands, as outlined in (cite: groe22).

No corrections were applied for data at wavelengths longer than 30 $\mu$m because $A_{\lambda}/A_{K_{\rm s}}$ is expected to be lower than 0.2, which would imply relatively small corrections even for the higher-extinction sources.

assumptions.value: Single pulsation period assumed in light curve fitting

evidence.quote: The $K_{\rm s}$-band light curves have been analysed using the codes and methodology outlined in (cite: groeetal20) assuming a single period.

fitting.value: Light-curve period fitting following (cite: groeetal20) and (cite: groe22)

evidence.quote: The $K_{\rm s}$-band light curves have been analysed using the codes and methodology outlined in (cite: groeetal20) assuming a single period.

validation.value: Compared derived periods across Ks, W1, and W2 bands and against literature periods where available

evidence.quote: The results, including the adopted period are collected in Table \[t:summary_periods\] that also cites periods found in the literature.

analysis_steps.goal: Model dust continuum SEDs to derive luminosities, dust mass-loss rates, and CSE inner radii

method.value: Fit dust radiative transfer models using MCMax to extinction-corrected photometry at wavelengths > 1 um, and integrate the fitted SED over wavelength using the adopted distance to derive stellar luminosity and dust mass-loss rate.

evidence.quote: To reproduce the SED of each source, we calculated radiative transfer models using the code MCMax (cite: minetal09) assuming spherical symmetry of the dust CSEs.

In the fitting procedure, we only include photometric points for wavelengths larger than 1 $\mu$m because of the large extinction towards some of the sources and the relatively small contribution to the total luminosity of the emission at optical wavelengths.
The stellar luminosity is obtained by integrating the fit to the SED over wavelength and using the distance to the given source.

key_parameters.value: Grain size distribution power-law index = -3.5, a_min = 0.001 um, a_max = 1.0 um; R_out = 10000 au; initial T_* = 2500 K; T_d(R_in) = 1000 K (for standard envelopes)

evidence.quote: We consider astronomical silicate grains (cite: osseetal92) with a number size distribution given by a power law with index $-$3.5 and minimum and maximum grains sizes equal to 0.001 $\mu$m and 1.0 $\mu$m, respectively.

claims.hypothesis: High-mass-loss-rate OH/IR stars in the inner Galactic Bulge descend from solar-type progenitors near the tip of the AGB rather than massive AGB stars.
claims.experiment: Construct extinction-corrected SEDs from multi-wavelength archival photometry, fit dust radiative transfer models with MCMax, integrate SEDs assuming the 8.2 kpc GC distance, and compare derived luminosities with stellar evolution tracks.
claims.result: 17 stars have luminosities consistent with the inner GB, with a median luminosity of 5600 L_odot (range 2100-8700 L_odot, plus two outliers at 25000 L_odot), corresponding to initial masses of 1.2-1.6 M_odot and ages of 4-7 Gyr.
claims.finding: The inner-Galactic-Bulge OH/IR stars descend from solar-type stars (1.2-1.6 M_odot) and lie near the tip of the AGB, below the mass threshold for hot-bottom burning.

evidence.quote: The median luminosity of the inner-Galactic-Bulge sub-sample, 5600 $L_\odot$, corresponds to an initial mass in the range 1.2 $-$ 1.6 $M_\odot$, indicating that these inner-Galactic-Bulge OH/IR stars descend from solar-type stars.
This means that these objects will not become carbon stars, and their masses fall well below the limit for the hot-bottom-burning (HBB) process.

claims.hypothesis: A subset of inner-GB OH/IR stars has recently ceased mass loss and begun evolving beyond the tip of the AGB.
claims.experiment: Fit SEDs with MCMax allowing for detached dust shells and warmer central stars, and compare SED classes with pulsation variability from VVV and WISE light curves and ALMA CO morphology.
claims.result: Six of the 17 inner-GB objects require detached dust shells (R_in = 200-600 au, corresponding to <=150 yr) and warmer central stars (3500-5000 K), lack Mira-like periodicity, and include the only two sources with resolved bipolar/cavity CO structures.
claims.finding: DE-type objects have recently ceased or strongly decreased their mass loss and are evolving off the AGB on a rapid transition timescale (~100 yr).

evidence.quote: These characteristics strongly indicate that the DE objects are the most evolved in our total sample, that is they lie close to the tip of the AGB, and in some cases may even have left the AGB.

The two classes appear to be rather distinct, and this suggests that the transition from one stage to the other is fast, of the order $\ensuremath{\lesssim}$ 100 yr, if our evolutionary interpretation is correct.

claims.hypothesis: Inner-GB OH/IR stars experience intense mass loss, high expansion velocities, and low 12CO/13CO ratios established on the RGB rather than via hot-bottom burning.
claims.experiment: Observe 12CO(2-1), 12CO(3-2), and 13CO(3-2) with ALMA and model velocity-integrated fluxes with a non-LTE Monte Carlo radiative transfer code.
claims.result: For the inner-GB sample, the median gas mass-loss rate is 2e-5 M_odot yr^-1, median expansion velocity is 18 km s^-1, median gas-to-dust ratio (SE sources) is 200, and median 12CO/13CO ratio is 5.
claims.finding: The stars lie at the high end of AGB mass-loss rate and expansion velocity distributions (indicating non-low metallicity), and their very low inferred 12C/13C ratios (~5) must arise from first dredge-up plus extra mixing on the RGB since their masses are too low for hot-bottom burning.

evidence.quote: The median gas-mass-loss rate, gas terminal expansion velocity, gas-to-dust mass ratio, and circumstellar $^{12}$CO/$^{13}$CO abundance ratio have been estimated to be 2$\times$10$^{-5}$ $M_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$, 18 km s$^{-1}$, 200 (excluding the sources with detached dust envelopes, which show markedly lower gas-to-dust ratios), and 5, respectively, for the inner-Galactic-Bulge sub-sample.

The inferred very low stellar $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C isotope ratios are indicative of CNO-cycle nuclear processing, and they are most likely established at the surfaces of the stars during the first dredge-up on the red giant branch since these stars are not expected to experience hot-bottom burning.

claims.hypothesis: A stronger interstellar UV radiation field in the inner Galactic Bulge significantly alters the CO photodissociation radii, source sizes, and derived mass-loss rates, while truncating the OH maser shells.
claims.experiment: Perform radiative transfer sensitivity tests varying the CO photodissociation radius R_1/2 and compare with observed Gaussian source sizes and OH shell models.
claims.result: Decreasing R_1/2 by a factor of 3 lowers CO(2-1) and CO(3-2) fluxes by 34% and 6% (~20% mass-loss underestimate), and deconvolved Gaussian sizes are insensitive to R_1/2 unless reduced by a factor of 10; an OH shell 3x smaller (~700 au) matches the maximum observed detached dust inner radius (600 au).
claims.finding: A higher UV field in the inner GB does not significantly affect the CO mass-loss rate or 12CO/13CO estimates, nor can R_1/2 be constrained from the Gaussian sizes, whereas stronger continuum UV photodissociation of H2O/OH shrinks the OH shell to ~700 au, explaining the absence of OH/IR stars with dust inner radii >600 au.

evidence.quote: Consequently, the UV radiation field in the inner GB must be substantially higher than that in the solar neighbourhood to have any effect on our estimated mass-loss rates.
Thus, we can conclude that our estimated source sizes, in all likelihood, give no information on the photodissociation radius.

An OH shell about three times smaller than that obtained for a solar neighbourhood UV radiation field, that is about 700 au for our median values of mass-loss rate and expansion velocity, fits very well a scenario where sources with CSE inner radii in excess of $\approx$ 700 au would not be detectable as OH/IR stars, and hence not end up in our sample.

why_this_data.value: CO rotational lines provide mass-loss rates and 12C/13C isotopic ratios that OH masers cannot, and ALMA's high sensitivity and interferometric spatial filtering suppress ubiquitous extended interstellar CO contamination along lines of sight toward the inner Galactic Bulge.

evidence.quote: The OH maser emission provides interesting insights for studying OH/IR stars, but only brings (at best) order-of-magnitude estimates of the mass-loss rate, and no information on elemental isotopic ratios, such as $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C, which are key signposts of stellar evolution. Observations of rotational lines from carbon monoxide (CO) have proven to be essential in this context (cite: schoolof01; debeetal10; ramsolof14).

Observing OH/IR stars in CO line radiation towards regions of high extinction is a difficult task due to the contamination of ubiquitous interstellar CO along the line of sight. At the distance of the GC this is further exacerbated by the weakness of the circumstellar line and continuum radiation. Nevertheless, through the use of the ALMA interferometer both of these problems have been, at least partly, circumvented
